claim: Real analyst forecasts on short horizons are highly discriminating and well calibrated: ROC area 0.940, Brier 0.074, 76% outcome variance explained (N=1,514, one Canadian unit, 59% under 6 months). Robust to ambiguous-outcome coding (Brier 0.090-0.097).
agent_test: Report AUC, Brier and calibration separately for the agent on a short-horizon set; compare with a one-shot baseline at equal tokens.
audit_note: Mandel and Barnes numbers verified (N=1,514, A=0.940, Brier 0.074, eta2 0.758, sensitivity 0.090/0.097, Canadian IAS); the 59% under 6 months / 96% under a year comes from the Tetlock and Mellers reply, not Mandel and Barnes itself. Minor: the 1,514 exclusions are team forecasts and missing data; ambiguous outcomes were dropped earlier.

claim: Tetlock and Mellers (2014) argue that the analysts' strong Brier scores partly reflect an easy question mix: short horizons (59% under 6 months) and many near-certain questions (over half scored Brier 0 or 0.01), whereas Tetlock's weak results were mostly long-range; Mandel and Barnes found no significant effect of time frame on discrimination. Raw Brier is not comparable across question sets with different base rates (Paleka et al. 2025).
agent_test: Score the agent on a base-rate-stratified set; report Brier skill vs a base-rate forecaster, not raw Brier.
audit_note: Tetlock and Mellers (a06/b07 are the same reply) only argue that the analyst questions were short-range and mostly near-certain (59% under 6 months, over half Brier 0 or 0.01); Mandel and Barnes themselves found time frame had no significant effect on discrimination, so stating it as an established question-mix effect is too strong. Paleka (worked example, Brier not comparable across base rates) is verified.
claim_before_audit: The high analyst score is partly a question-mix effect: short horizons and many low-variance questions. Tetlock weak results were mostly long-range. Raw Brier is not comparable across question sets.

claim: Analysts were underconfident (signed deviation -0.076), worse on harder and more important questions, unaffected by experience. A one-parameter transform (a=2.2) cut calibration index 0.016 to 0.0018 and absolute deviation 12.7% to 4.2% (fitted in-sample).
agent_test: Fit a recalibration map on a held-out half of agent forecasts, test on the other half; compare ECE at equal tokens.

claim: Seniority and easier questions raise discrimination (0.951 vs 0.909; 0.966 vs 0.913); importance and time frame do not.
agent_test: Check whether agent AUC drops on harder questions as sharply as humans (0.966 to 0.913).

claim: Aggregating and extremizing forecasts improves accuracy when individual forecasts are underconfident (conditions apply). Tournament teams, training and tracking helped: training +6-11% per year; teams beat independents each of 4 years; over half of gain was noise reduction.
agent_test: Run N samples of the agent; aggregate by median vs logit-mean vs extremized mean at equal total tokens.
audit_note: Mellers 2024 gives training +6-11% per year, teams better each of 4 years, over 50% noise reduction; Mellers 2014 confirms training/teaming/tracking; Satopaa and Ungar abstract supports extremizing (conditions not in abstract); Mandel and Tetlock confirm underconfidence and recalibration helped in IARPA ACE. Caveat: most sources come from the same GJP-linked group (Mellers, Ungar, Tetlock, Baron), Mandel being the independent voice.

claim: Coherence and consistency relate to accuracy only weakly or conditionally in humans: r=0.37 in poker experts, 0.06 in amateurs; no separation of better and worse analysts in Dhami et al. 2024.
agent_test: Measure correlation of agent coherence violations with Brier on resolved questions.

claim: LLM consistency (arbitrage) scores correlate with Brier (R 0.85-0.92 for some checks, little for others), but optimising on checks did not generalise to held-out checks or improve Brier.
agent_test: Use consistency as a no-label proxy only; verify it predicts Brier on held-out checks.

claim: LLM forecasters trail the human crowd on real-question sets: Halawi's retrieval-augmented, fine-tuned system scored Brier 0.179 vs crowd 0.149 (N=914 test questions) and its best no-retrieval baseline 0.208; the best Autocast model reached 65% accuracy vs 92% for the crowd; in Schoenegger and Park (2023) GPT-4 scored 0.20 vs crowd 0.07 (N=23 questions, GPT-4 not statistically different from 0.25).
agent_test: Baseline: agent without retrieval on a frozen post-cutoff set; expect near 0.21-0.25.
audit_note: Numbers verified (Halawi .179 vs .149 N=914, best baseline .208; Autocast 65% vs 92%, Halawi cites 65.4 vs 92.8; Schoenegger-Park .20 vs .07 N=23, GPT-4 not distinct from .25). But the Halawi 'system' is retrieval-augmented and fine-tuned, and Autocast models are fine-tuned retrieval-based T5/FiD, so they are not 'un-augmented LLM forecasters'; only the .208 baseline and S&P GPT-4 are un-augmented.
claim_before_audit: Un-augmented LLM forecasters trail the human crowd on real-question sets: Halawi system 0.179 vs crowd 0.149 (N=914); best no-retrieval baseline 0.208; Autocast 65% vs 92%; Schoenegger-Park 2023 GPT-4 0.20 vs crowd 0.07 (N=23).

claim: Retrieval plus fine-tuned reasoning closes most but not all of the gap: 0.206 with neither vs 0.179 full; removing only one costs 0.002-0.007. Averaging system and crowd beats both (0.146).
schema_part: S (evidence gathering) / O (combine with outside prior)
agent_test: Ablate retrieval vs reasoning prompt separately at equal tokens.

claim: By 2025 frontier reasoning LLMs reach or pass the human crowd on average (o3 0.1352 vs crowd 0.149; Sonnet 4 0.156 pastcasting), but superforecasters stay ahead (ForecastBench 0.096 vs best LLM 0.122; gap 0.054 > GPT-4 to GPT-4o 0.026). UPDATE (gap search): by July 2026 the ForecastBench organisers report scaffolded systems statistically indistinguishable from superforecasters (K22), so 'superforecasters stay ahead' now holds only for plain models and early-2025 bots.
agent_test: Track agent Brier against a superforecaster-level reference on a dynamic question set.

claim: Lu (2025) LLM-vs-expert comparison is weak: expert median Brier 0.0225 is set against model mean 0.1352; expert mean was 0.1573 (N=157), worse than o3. Not evidence that experts beat o3.
agent_test: Always compare like with like (mean vs mean, same questions).

claim: Ensembling LLM forecasts helps: 12-model LLM crowd 0.20 matches human crowd 0.19 (equivalence not preregistered); averaging model with human median beats the model updating on it (0.13 vs 0.14-0.17). Ensembles help agents (SD 0.092) but not base GPT-4o (0.218 vs 0.210).
agent_test: Compare single run, same-model vote and mixed-prompt vote at equal tokens.
audit_note: Silicon crowd (12 LLMs, .20 vs .19, p=.850; equivalence non-preregistered; averaging .13/.14 vs updated forecasts, p=.011/.001) and Hsieh et al. (.169 vs .180 agents, .218 vs .210 base GPT-4o, SD .092 vs .150) verified. Minor slip: '0.14-0.17' mixes pre-update (.17) and post-update (.14) GPT-4 scores; 'help agents (SD 0.092)' means lower variance, Brier gain is .169 vs .180.

claim: LLMs show acquiescence bias: mean prediction 57.35% vs 50 (t=86.2), and Resolve-Yes items score much worse than Resolve-No. UPDATE (gap search): not general. Pratt found low-probability guessing, AIA reports hedging toward 0.5, and o1 and Llama had mean forecasts of 41.5-44.8% on a 100-question set. No negation-pair or priming test found.
agent_test: Check agent mean forecast against base rate; test with negated question pairs.

claim: Adding forecasting strategies to prompts did not help: the plain prompt beat all strategy variants (Pratt 2024); narrative prompts were worse than direct (Lu 2025).
agent_test: Test plain vs scaffolded prompts on forecasting at equal tokens.
audit_note: Pratt et al. (2024): plain prompt outperformed all strategy prompts and the human market baseline; Lu (2025, single author, GMU): narrative prompts worse than direct. Narrative framing is not strictly a 'forecasting strategy' but the wording is acceptable.

claim: Outcome-based RL improves forecast calibration (Brier 0.190 vs o1 0.202, ECE 0.062 vs 0.093; Phi-4 0.200 vs base 0.221 vs control 0.214) but the market price still wins by 0.039.
agent_test: Not testable in a scaffold; use as upper reference.
audit: downgraded 2026-10-31 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: LLM assistants improve human forecasts (24-28% accuracy gain, N=991), even a noisy overconfident assistant; humans did not discriminate good advice from bad.
agent_test: Test whether the agent over-defers to a supplied crowd prior when that prior is noisy.
audit: downgraded 2026-10-31 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Persuasiveness of rationales is not tied to forecast accuracy (beta 0.007, BF10 0.024); confident style r=-0.02, insistent style r=-0.38 with accuracy.
agent_test: Check the agent's rationale confidence vs actual accuracy.

claim: LLM forecast benchmarks are leaky: at least 3.8% early-resolving questions, date-restricted search leaks post-date text, Brier overweights high-base-rate questions.
agent_test: Use pastcasting with frozen retrieval and base-rate stratification.
audit_note: Paleka et al.: at least 3.8% of Halawi questions resolved early, search leak example ('jan 6' before 2020), Brier not comparable across base rates (worked example verified). Alur et al. independently document search foreknowledge leakage (about 1.65% of results; 17% of queries in one case) though they find it moves their ForecastBench Brier by under 0.001. Four of the listed sources are the same Paleka paper.

claim: Benchmark progress is steady: ForecastBench Brier tracks Arena score (r=-0.68) and log compute (r=-0.67); parity extrapolated near Arena 1406 (CI 1346-1633). Small N, wide CI.
agent_test: Re-fit with newer models.

claim: Precision matters: finer-grained probabilities were more accurate (888,328 forecasts); at least four categories raised accuracy.
agent_test: Compare coarse 5-bucket vs 1% outputs from the agent.
audit: downgraded 2026-10-31 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Statistical or algorithmic combination beats human intuition only modestly overall (d=0.12, clinical vs statistical).
agent_test: Low priority.

claim: Parity with superforecasters on ForecastBench is claimed for scaffolded systems in 2026 but is a non-rejection of equality, not a win: one-sided p-values 0.41 (Cassi AI), 0.14-0.16 (xAI, DeepMind); human baselines date from July 2024; the AIA Forecaster scored 0.1076 vs superforecasters 0.1110 on FB-7-21. Early-2025 bots still lost to Pros (head-to-head -17.7, CI -28.3 to -7.0).
agent_test: Re-check after the fall 2026 superforecaster round.

claim: In the studies read, single-paragraph strategy prompts moved Brier by about 0.01 at best (frequency-based, base-rate-first, chain-of-thought, step-back), Bayesian-reasoning and propose-evaluate-select prompts hurt, and compound prompts gave no robust gain (Schoenegger et al. 2025); the gains from scaffolds came mainly from search (agentic search 0.1140 vs 0.1230 without news), sampling and aggregation (10-sample mean 0.1140 vs single 0.1182; Alur et al. 2025), and fine-tuning in Halawi et al.; no equal-token comparison exists.
schema_part: S (reference-class and search steps); O (do not add verbal Bayes)
agent_test: Run plain vs base-rate-first vs 5-sample mean at equal tokens.
audit_note: Numbers verified (Schoenegger et al.: best prompts about -0.014 to -0.011, Bayesian Reasoning and Propose-Evaluate-Select significantly worse; Alur et al.: agentic search 0.1140 vs 0.1230 no-news, single forecast 0.1182 vs 10-sample mean 0.1140). But 'only through search, sampling and aggregation' is a universal claim; the sources test prompts and search/aggregation, not other routes, and Halawi's fine-tuning also lowered Brier (.206 to .186).
claim_before_audit: A scaffold beats a plain prompt only through search, sampling and aggregation, not through reasoning instructions. Single-paragraph strategy prompts moved Brier about 0.01 at best (base rate, frequency format, step-back); Bayesian-update and propose-then-select prompts hurt; stacking best prompts gave nothing; agentic search 0.1140 vs 0.1230 without search. No equal-token comparison exists.

claim: Averaging independent samples from the same agent is a strong baseline: mean, trimmed mean and median are equal within 0.0004 Brier at 10 samples; most gain arrives by 5 samples (single forecast 0.1182 vs mean 0.1140). An LLM that reads all samples and writes one forecast is worse than the mean; a supervisor with fresh search and a confidence gate is slightly better (0.1125).
schema_part: O (sample and pool); not a synthesiser step
agent_test: Test mean vs logit mean vs supervisor at a fixed token budget.

claim: Post-hoc log-odds stretching of the pooled LLM forecast helps: Brier 0.1140 to 0.1085 (fixed d=3) and 0.1076 (Platt, coefficient about 1.73); a coefficient fitted on another benchmark gave 0.1104 vs 0.1125 unstretched, so it transfers but loses part of the gain. Optimum for AIA 2.27, for superforecasters 1.72. It helps only if the call is on the right side of 0.5, and likely less for newer, better-calibrated models (ECE about 0.04).
schema_part: G (calibration step on the pooled answer)
agent_test: Fit the stretch on the agent's own resolved questions; compare fixed 1.7 vs fitted.

claim: Crowd or market prior in the prompt helps (Brier 0.116 to 0.103 without search; 0.085 to 0.075 with) but largely substitutes for search, and an LLM that sees the price can score worse than the price (0.109 vs 0.096 in the earlier ForecastBench). Over-deference when the prior is wrong was not tested directly.
schema_part: S (prior step, with a check that the answer adds information)
agent_test: Give a wrong prior on a held-out set and measure the damage.

claim: Leakage is controllable: a judged audit found about 1.65% of search results leaked the outcome and removing flagged questions moved Brier only 0.0002-0.0007, but gpt-oss-120b looked best (0.1076) only by exploiting leaks (17.09% of its queries, 57% of the benchmark). Cleanest tests are live, forward-resolving questions.
agent_test: Log retrieved document dates in all agent runs.

claim: No independent replication of Mandel and Barnes 2014 in another agency or country was found. The nearest evidence is an internal extension (3,622 forecasts, 2,013 codable; same underconfidence and skill) and UK analyst studies that test other things (ACH failed; coherentizing plus averaging cut MAE 61%).
agent_test: Look for Dutch, UK or Australian forecast archives.

claim: Numbers beat words for communicating probabilities: numeric and combined formats beat verbal on all three agreement measures (N=1,202), and 44% of Canadian analyst forecasts could not be coded because of vague language. LLMs map verbal phrases to numbers like humans on average but shift by 7.0 points with prior belief. No study scores LLM verbal forecasts against outcomes.
agent_test: Compare word-first vs number-first forecasts from the agent on resolved questions.

claim: A label-free quality signal exists for human forecasts: an LLM-scored rationale rubric gives r=.19 at forecast level and r=.51 at forecaster level (55,000 pairs), and 9 quick calibration questions give r=.27 with a hard forecast. Both are modest and unvalidated for agent traces; LLM consistency checks did not generalise to held-out checks (K07).
agent_test: Score the agent's own rationales and test against resolved outcomes.

claim: Clean live evidence for late 2025: frontier reasoning LLMs match the market in Brier (GPT-5 0.184 vs market 0.187, 1,367 Kalshi events, 76% sports) and calibrate better (ECE about 0.04 vs 0.067), but still fail to make money; agents trail sell-side analysts (win rate 33% at best).
agent_test: Repeat on a political-events set.
